lesson_title: Two Buckets a Day — How a City Nearly Ran Dry
hook_text: In 2018 Cape Town published the date its taps would be turned off. Then it beat the date.
clip_script: Early 2018. Three winters of rain have failed, Cape Town's dams are sliding toward 13 percent, and the city publishes an actual date — Day Zero — when household taps will be closed and every resident will queue for 25 litres a day. Twenty-five litres is two buckets. One short shower uses more. Now here is what makes this a geography lesson and not just a scare story. Drought is not simply low rainfall — the Karoo lives happily on 300 millimetres a year. Drought is the salary a place was built on suddenly failing, and it collapses in a fixed order: first the rain, then the soil, then the rivers and dams, then people's jobs, prices and lives. Cape Town was at the last stage. And the city fought back with behaviour, not magic: two-minute showers, greywater on the garden, brutal tariffs on heavy users, pressure turned down in the pipes, a dashboard shaming every suburb's usage. Water use fell from about 1 200 million litres a day toward 500 — the city cut itself in half. Day Zero kept retreating until the 2018 rains finally washed it away. The taps never closed. Remember both halves: the danger was completely real, and human behaviour actually beat it.
visual_style: A dam gauge dropping toward a red 13 percent line while a countdown calendar flips toward Day Zero, cut against two buckets on a doorstep, then the usage graph bending down from 1 200 to 500 as the countdown reverses.
mood: Tense true-story build with a genuinely earned win.
pacing: Urgent open on the countdown, methodical middle through the four stages, accelerating relief as the graph bends.
